use_case.name: Read lab requisition forms
use_case.summary: Extract the fields from faxed and scanned requisition forms, pre-fill the LIMS record, and have accessioning staff confirm it instead of typing it. About 2,300 forms a day from 1,400 clinics, each with its own layout.

intake.problem: Samples wait in a queue until their paper requisition form is keyed by hand, which delays results and causes keying errors.
intake.who: Nine accessioning staff at three labs; clinics waiting for results.
intake.today: Staff key each faxed or scanned form into LIMS, about 4 minutes a form. 30% of orders come through a structured web portal instead.
intake.cost: 3.1% keying error rate (last quarter's audit); about 40 wrong-test re-runs a week at $85 each; results 6 to 8 hours late on busy mornings.
intake.wrong_answer: Wrong test runs or the result goes to the wrong clinic. Staff confirm every record; unsure fields are highlighted.
intake.data: 1.9 million scanned forms over three years, each linked to the LIMS record keyed from it. LIMS read replica in Azure. Pet owners' names, addresses and phones; no human medical data.
intake.value: Median receipt-to-in-testing time: 3.4 hours today, target under 1 hour. Fewer re-runs.
intake.sign_off: Marcus Reyes (lab operations, owner), Priya Natarajan (CEO, sponsor), IT security lead, compliance manager.

input.evidence: Faxed and scanned paper, many handwritten, about 1,400 different clinic layouts.

rules.evidence: Where each field sits differs by clinic and by hand; staff read the form, they don't follow rules.

output.evidence: Values extracted from unstructured images: species, tests, clinic, vet, owner contact.

alternative.evidence: The web portal already takes 30% of orders and has been pushed for years; rural clinics and referral labs stay on paper, so it solves well under 40% of today's paper volume.

alternative.description: Grow the clinic web portal past its 30% share: onboarding calls for the top 100 paper clinics and a tick-box fax form for the 50 most-ordered tests. Keep doing this alongside the build; every portal order skips extraction entirely.

value.evidence: Median receipt-to-in-testing time, 3.4 hours today; plus about $3,400 a week in wrong-test re-runs.

volume.evidence: 2,300 forms a day from LIMS counts; 4 minutes a form; 40 re-runs a week at $85.

owner.evidence: Marcus Reyes owns the process and outcome; the CEO sponsors it with budget set aside.

wrong_answer.evidence: Cost is known (wrong test, wrong clinic). Staff confirm every record and low-confidence fields are highlighted.

availability.evidence: 1.9 million scans, each linked to the LIMS record keyed from it: three years of right answers to test against.

quality.evidence: Not profiled yet. The keyed records carry the known 3.1% error rate, so they are noisy as answers; audited forms can serve as a clean test set.

access.evidence: Marcus Reyes owns LIMS and the document store; read-only access to both already exists in Azure for reporting.

sensitivity.evidence: Owner contact data (PII) is already in a restricted LIMS table and masked in logs. Processing stays in their Azure tenant under terms that exclude training. Animal records are not PHI.

regulations: State consumer privacy laws for pet owners' contact data

sign_off.needs: Data-flow diagram from scan to model to LIMS, Azure tenant and model deployment settings, who can see the confirm screen, and how prompts, images and outputs are logged and retained.
Which owner contact fields are extracted, retention for images and model logs, and the confirm-every-record design.
Field-level accuracy on audited forms, the confirm screen, and the fallback to typing.
The turnaround metric, baseline, target and check date.

reasons: The inputs are scans of about 1,400 different, often handwritten forms, so no fixed template or rule set can read them; this is the kind of work a model is for.
The value is measurable today: median receipt-to-in-testing time is 3.4 hours against a 1-hour target, and wrong-test re-runs cost about $3,400 a week.
Three years of scans already linked to keyed records give a ready-made test set, and the data sits with a clear owner and an existing read path.
Owner contact data is already restricted and masked, and processing stays in Ridgeline's own Azure tenant, so the main sign-off questions have answers.
Data quality is the softest score: it hasn't been profiled, and the keyed records include the 3.1% error rate. Profile a sample in week one.

top_risks.risk: Accuracy on poor faxes and handwriting is too low for confirming to beat typing.
top_risks.mitigation: Measure field-level accuracy on 500 audited forms before building the screen; send low-confidence forms straight to manual keying.

top_risks.risk: Staff wave through pre-filled fields, so errors that typing would catch get saved.
top_risks.mitigation: Require explicit confirmation of species and test codes, highlight unsure fields, and audit a weekly sample against today's 3.1%.

top_risks.risk: The keyed records used as answers carry their own errors, so accuracy looks better or worse than it is.
top_risks.mitigation: Build the test set only from forms checked in last quarter's audit.

first_build.scope: One lab, the 50 clinics that send the most paper (about 40% of its paper volume), plus referral-lab forms. Extract clinic, vet, species, animal ID, tests and owner contact; pre-fill LIMS; staff confirm every record. Run it for eight weeks next to the current process.
first_build.left_out: The other two labs, free-text clinical history, saving without confirmation, and any change to how samples are routed.

measure.metric: Median time from sample receipt to in testing, at the pilot lab
measure.target: under 1 hour, with the keying error rate at or below 3.1%

result.human_review: A person reviews outputs below a confidence threshold, plus a sample of the rest.
